dek_candidates: In an oversubscribed Indian IPO, every retail applicant has the same shot—whether they bid for one lot or fourteen. Here is how the allotment is engineered.
design_notes: Intro should open with a short, concrete example (one-lot vs fourteen-lot) to immediately convey the lottery principle.
Retail allotment section must present the worked example verbatim (with proper attribution) to establish authority.
The NII sub-split section is short; can be merged with 'Allocation categories' if tighter structure preferred, but kept separate for clarity of the 2022 change.
SCSB compensation is a brief sidebar; consider placing it as a standalone section after retail allotment or as a highlighted box.
No bulletpoint thicket: use tables for comparisons; write prose for narratives.
Every claim is sourced; no phantom numbers.

beats.beat: Detail Reg 32(1) percentages: not less than 35% retail, not less than 15% NII, not more than 50% QIB; mutual fund reservation of 5% within QIB.
Explain that under-subscription in retail or NII can spill over to other categories (provided provisos).
Note the special case for loss-making issuers (Reg 32(2)): retail capped at 10%, NII at 15%, QIB at 75%.

allocation-categories.heading: The three buckets: QIB, NII, retail
allocation-categories.purpose: Walk through the base allocation rules and how the net offer is carved among investor categories.

beats.beat: Define anchor investor: QIB with minimum application of ₹10 crore (mainboard book-built).
Up to 60% of QIB portion can go to anchor investors (Reg 32(3)).
Anchor investor allocation is discretionary; limits on number of investors based on total anchor size (Schedule XIII, Sec 10(c)).
One-third of anchor portion reserved for domestic mutual funds (Schedule XIII, Sec 10(d)).
Lock-in: 50% for 90 days, 50% for 30 days (from April 2022 amendment; footnote 725).
Anchor bidding opens one day before issue; price discovery and payment mechanics (Schedule XIII, Sec 10(e)-(h)).

anchor-investors.heading: Anchor investors: carving out the QIB portion
anchor-investors.purpose: Explain how anchor investors (up to 60% of QIB portion) are allocated, their minimum ticket, mutual fund reservation, and lock-in.

beats.beat: Employee reservation: aggregate not exceeding 5% of post-issue capital; value per employee not exceeding ₹2 lakh (may go to ₹5 lakh if under-subscription in employee portion and proportionate allocation).
Shareholder reservation: not exceeding 10% of issue size; only for shareholders of listed subsidiaries or listed promoter companies (not promoter group).
Unsubscribed portions in reserved categories may be adjusted inter se and then added to net offer.
No further application in net offer can be made by those who apply under reservation (except employees and retail individual shareholders).

employee-shareholder-reservations.heading: Reservation portions: employees and shareholders
employee-shareholder-reservations.purpose: Describe the caps and conditions for employee reservation (up to 5% of post-issue capital, value cap ₹2L per employee, with roll-up provision) and shareholder reservation (up to 10% of issue size).

beats.beat: Open mid-action with the lottery mechanic: in an oversubscribed retail category, applying for more lots does not improve odds.
State the headline allocation percentages (Reg 32(1)) for a normal book-built IPO: retail at least 35%, NII at least 15%, QIB at most 50% (with 5% reserved for mutual funds).
Mention the alternative compulsory-QIB book for loss-making issuers (Reg 32(2)): only 10% retail, 15% NII, 75% QIB.

intro.purpose: Set up the core insight: Indian retail allotment is a lottery, not a market, and explain why that matters.

beats.beat: Reg 32(3A): one-third of NII portion reserved for applicants with application size >₹2L up to ₹10L (sHNI); two-thirds for >₹10L (bHNI).
Effective date: April 1, 2022 for issues opening on or after that date (footnote 83); for issues ≥₹10,000 crore, effective July 1, 2022.
Unsubscribed portion in one sub-category may spill to the other.

In case of oversubscription within either sub-category, allotment follows the same lottery principle as retail (though the corpus does not explicitly spell out a worked example for NII, the regulation implies proportionate/lottery based on scheme of allotment; we note this is inferred from the general principle).

nii-split.heading: The NII sub-split: sHNI and bHNI
nii-split.purpose: Explain the split of the NII bucket into two sub-categories (sHNI ₹2–10L, bHNI >₹10L), effective April 2022, and how draw of lots works if oversubscribed.

beats.beat: Definition of retail individual investor: bid value not more than ₹2 lakh (Reg 2(vv)).
Undersubscribed case: every applicant gets at least the minimum bid lot; remaining shares distributed proportionally (Example A paraphrased).

Oversubscribed case (Example B from Schedule XIII): 35 lakh shares on offer, 2 lakh applicants, minimum lot 20 shares. The maximum number of allottees is 1,75,000 (35,00,000 / 20). Allotment is by lottery, with each successful applicant receiving exactly the minimum lot. The remaining 25,000 get nothing.
The lottery is applied proportionally across all bid-lot tiers: the same 87.5% success rate for 1-lot bidders and for 16-lot bidders. No advantage for larger bids.
The principle: fairness by design — size does not increase probability.

retail-allotment.heading: Retail allotment: undersubscribed vs. oversubscribed
retail-allotment.purpose: Describe the two cases with the verbatim SEBI worked examples from Schedule XIII; show that oversubscription triggers a lottery where each successful applicant gets exactly one minimum lot.

beats.beat: SEBI recognized opportunity loss scenarios: SCSB failure to bid, failure to process, or other errors leading to rejection (Master Circular Ch.5, para 1).
Compensation formula: (Listing price - Issue price) × shares that would have been allotted × probability of allotment (para 3).
For issues subscribed 90-100%, compensation equals full allotment loss (para 4). No compensation if listing price below issue price (para 5).
Applicant must seek redress with SCSB within 3 months of listing; SCSB must resolve within 15 days or pay 15% p.a. interest (para 7-8).

scsb-compensation.heading: When the bank fails: compensation for ASBA errors
scsb-compensation.purpose: Explain the SEBI-mandated compensation formula for retail investors whose applications are rejected due to SCSB failure.
